claims.text: Randomized controlled trials evaluating online mental health services demonstrated no statistically significant change in help-seeking behavior compared to control groups.
A quasi-experimental evaluation of an online mental health educational game found a statistically significant increase in willingness to seek help from pre-test to post-test.
Cross-sectional studies found that an average of 35% of users reported online mental health services facilitated seeking help from a professional source.
An online self-help cognitive behavioral therapy program produced a modest reduction in depressive symptoms in young adults post-test with an effect size of d = 0.20.
Only 22% of reviewed studies evaluating online mental health services utilized adequate measures of help-seeking.

evidence.description: Across three RCTs, no significant difference in mental health visits or formal/informal help-seeking behavior was found between intervention and control groups over time.

In Shandley et al., playing ReachOut Central led to an increase in willingness to seek help from pre-test (male mean 4.01, female mean 4.17) to post-test (male mean 4.39, female mean 5.04; F 1,264 = 18.04, P < .001).
Cross-sectional studies reported that online services facilitated seeking professional help for an average of 34.9% (range 6% to 75.8%) of users.
Clarke et al. reported a modest reduction in depressive symptoms post-test (N=160, d=0.20, 95% CI 0.00-0.50) following an online CBT self-help program.
Only 4 out of 18 (22%) included studies used adequate measures of help-seeking as a primary outcome.

methodologies.name: PRISMA Systematic Review
methodologies.description: A systematic literature review conducted according to PRISMA guidelines searching PubMed, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Library databases for studies evaluating online mental health services and help-seeking among young people.
conditions: Evaluated online mental health services and help-seeking outcomes

limitations.text: No statistical meta-analyses could be conducted due to the heterogeneity of study designs permitted in the inclusion criteria.
Only three randomized controlled trials met inclusion criteria, limiting strong causal inference regarding online service efficacy.
Prior studies in this domain frequently suffered from small sample sizes, lack of longitudinal follow-up, and reliance on non-validated, single-item help-seeking measures.

future_work.text: Conduct high-quality randomized controlled trials with large representative samples and longitudinal follow-up of 6 to 12 months to determine the efficacy of online mental health help-seeking services.
Develop and apply standardized, validated measures to assess help-seeking behavior, intentions, and client satisfaction in e-mental health evaluations.
Design and evaluate specifically tailored online mental health services for young men to improve their engagement and help-seeking rates.
